deep.reconstruction:
Title: 'On the integration of the equation dx dξ + dy dη + dz dζ = 0.'

Geometric setup. A surface S: F(x,y,z)=0 is given. A line through two infinitely near points of S has direction (1, dy/dx, dz/dx); the manuscript writes this line as z' = (dz/dx)x' + a, y' = (dy/dx)x' + b. A second surface S*: f(ξ,η,ζ)=0 is sought. Its line element has direction (dξ, dη, dζ). Points of the two surfaces are tacitly put in correspondence, with ξ, η, ζ functions of x, y. The angle φ between corresponding line elements satisfies

cos φ = (dx dξ + dy dη + dz dζ) / (sqrt(dx²+dy²+dz²) · sqrt(dξ²+dη²+dζ²)).

The requirement is φ = 90° for every direction of displacement. This gives

(1) dx dξ + dy dη + dz dζ = 0, i.e. dr·dr* = 0 in modern vector notation.

This is the modern equation of an infinitesimal (isometric) bending of S with velocity field r* = (ξ,η,ζ). Equivalently, S* is a surface whose corresponding line elements are everywhere orthogonal to those of S.

Task. Express ξ, η, ζ in terms of x, y so that (1) holds identically.

Notation (Gauss-era partials in parentheses). Write p = (dz/dx), q = (dz/dy). Then:
- dz = p dx + q dy;
- dξ = ξ_x dx + ξ_y dy;
- dη = η_x dx + η_y dy;
- dζ = π dξ + ρ dη, so ζ is regarded as a function of (ξ,η) with partials π, ρ.

Substitution into (1). Regroup as dξ(dx + π dz) + dη(dy + ρ dz) = 0:

{dx + πp dx + πq dy}{ξ_x dx + ξ_y dy} + {dy + ρp dx + ρq dy}{η_x dx + η_y dy} = 0.

This is a quadratic form A dx² + B dx dy + C dy² = 0. Because dx and dy are independent (the equation must hold for every dy/dx), A = B = C = 0.

The page computes:
- A = ξ_x + π p ξ_x + ρ p η_x = 0;
- C = η_y + π q ξ_y + ρ q η_y = 0.

[Mine] The middle coefficient, which the page sets aside, is
B = (1+πp) ξ_y + πq ξ_x + ρp η_y + (1+ρq) η_x.
The page says B = 0 will later be replaced by an equivalent condition. On the next page this becomes ξ_y + η_x = k_x q + k_y p.

[Mine, interpretive] Since ζ_x = π ξ_x + ρ η_x and ζ_y = π ξ_y + ρ η_y:
- A = ξ_x + p ζ_x, i.e. r_x·r*_x;
- C = η_y + q ζ_y, i.e. r_y·r*_y;
- B = ξ_y + η_x + p ζ_y + q ζ_x, i.e. r_x·r*_y + r_y·r*_x.
These are exactly the three linearized first-fundamental-form conditions of infinitesimal bending. The next page continues to ζ_x = −ξ_x/p and ζ_y = −η_y/q. It then introduces a potential k with ζ = −k, ξ_x = k_x p, η_y = k_y q, and goes on to integrability conditions.
errors: No algebraic errors on this page: A and C are correctly extracted from the product.
Notational looseness: the line equations for the second surface reuse the coordinates x', y', z' of the first, and the a, b are merely intercepts. Harmless.
Unstated assumption: a point-to-point correspondence between the two surfaces (ξ, η, ζ as functions of x, y). Without it, 'the angle between the two line elements' is not defined.

Representing ζ via dζ = π dξ + ρ dη tacitly assumes ξ, η are independent functions of (x,y). The next page divides by ξ_x η_y − η_x ξ_y and by p q. These non-degeneracy assumptions (p, q ≠ 0, non-zero Jacobian) are never stated.
The statement that B = 0 will be 'replaced by an equivalent' condition is deferred; the page itself gives no justification. The handwriting also looks like a neat copy, possibly not Gauss's own hand.

results.what: Condition that corresponding line elements of two surfaces in point correspondence are everywhere orthogonal: dx dξ + dy dη + dz dζ = 0.
results.modern_name: Equation of infinitesimal bending (infinitesimal isometric deformation); dr·dr* = 0, with r* the bending field or 'associated surface'.
results.usually_credited_to: Jellett (1849/1853, inextensible surfaces); systematic theory by Weingarten, Darboux (Leçons, t. IV), Bianchi, late 19th c.

results.what: Splitting the identity in dx, dy into three coefficient equations A=0, B=0, C=0, with A = r_x·r*_x and C = r_y·r*_y.
results.modern_name: Linearized first fundamental form conditions (δE = δF = δG = 0)

results.what: Angle between two line elements via the direction-cosine formula.

deep.surprise_reason: The page only sets up the equation and performs elementary coefficient extraction. The problem itself is the infinitesimal-bending equation, which pre-dates Gauss's death through Jellett (c. 1849) and lies close to Gauss's own 1827 work on bending. A Gauss-circle treatment would be a mildly notable unpublished detail, but nothing on this page goes beyond routine calculus. The neat hand also suggests a copy or a student's text rather than original Gauss work.

checkable.sympy: p,q,pi_,rho,xx,xy,ex,ey,dx,dy=symbols('p q pi_ rho xx xy ex ey dx dy'); E=expand((dx+pi_*(p*dx+q*dy))*(xx*dx+xy*dy)+(dy+rho*(p*dx+q*dy))*(ex*dx+ey*dy)); simplify(Poly(E,dx,dy).coeff_monomial(dx**2)-(xx+pi_*p*xx+rho*p*ex))==0
checkable.asserts: Coefficient A of dx^2 equals ξ_x + π p ξ_x + ρ p η_x, as on the page.
Coefficient C of dy^2 equals η_y + π q ξ_y + ρ q η_y, as on the page.
The omitted middle coefficient B (my reconstruction).
The substituted expression equals dx dξ + dy dη + dz dζ with dζ = ζ_x dx + ζ_y dy.
The π, ρ formulas on the next page follow correctly from A=0, C=0.
Next page's −dζ = (ξ_x/p)dx + (η_y/q)dy is consistent with A=0, C=0.

transcription_corrections: Line 1 of the setup: 'Het man nun noch' in some readings should be 'Hat man nun noch'; the provided transcription has it right.
Folio mark at top right: circled '2' with a struck-through older number ('48gt 2' / '48 / 2'), not part of the text.
In the first line equation the image shows y' = (dy/dx) x' + b (written with a slightly ∂-like d); there is no partial notation distinction.
dζ = π dξ + ρ dη: the second Greek letter is a varrho (ϱ), correctly given.
